# Scarlet fever

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Scarlet fever*

[Original Article Link](/library/F40gOT)

---

## Summary

Scarlet <u>fever</u> is an acute syndrome caused by <u>Streptococcus pyogenes</u>, a highly contagious toxin-producing <u>group A Streptococcus</u> (<u>GAS</u>). The syndrome most commonly occurs in children and in less than 10% of patients with <u>streptococcal</u> tonsillopharyngitis. Scarlet <u>fever</u> classically manifests with <u>fever</u>, pharyngeal <u>erythema</u>, flushed cheeks with perioral <u>pallor</u>, <u>strawberry tongue</u>, and an <u>erythematous</u> <u>rash</u> with sandpaper-like texture. Desquamation of the face, trunk, hands, fingers, and toes begins approx. one week after the <u>rash</u> resolves. <u>Antibiotic</u> treatment with <u>penicillin</u> is recommended as scarlet <u>fever</u> may progress to severe disease and lead to complications (e.g., <u>rheumatic fever</u> and <u>poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis</u>). Recurrent infection with other toxins may occur as <u>S. pyogenes</u> produces several types of erythrogenic toxins.




![Scarlet fever fact sheet](media/mhd5kkomy6es73j4pico72cn.jpg)

Scarlet fever fact sheet

---

## Etiology

* Pathogenic

* <u>Group A Streptococcus</u> (i.e., <u>S. pyogenes</u>) produces <u>erythrogenic exotoxin A</u>, B, and/or C.

* Previous infection does not rule out additional episodes of the disease as there are several different types of scarlet <u>fever</u> toxin.

* Route of transmission: aerosol

* <u>Incubation period</u>:  2–5 days [[2]](/library/Bedza60)





References:[[3]](/library/NdY-JL)

---

## Clinical features

### <u>Prodrome</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Symptoms of tonsillopharyngitis</u>, e.g.: 

* <u>Sore throat</u> and difficulty <u>swallowing</u>

* Pharyngeal <u>erythema</u>, possibly with tonsillar <u>exudates</u>

* Enlarged cervical <u>lymph nodes</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, and/or <u>vomiting</u> [[4]](/library/m6dVlI0)





> [!TIP]
> Rarely, scarlet <u>fever</u> develops after a <u>streptococcal</u> <u>skin and soft tissue infection</u> rather than tonsillopharyngitis. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)




![Acute tonsillopharyngitis](media/u2ftbja64tvpydixqk8mr37o.jpg)

Acute tonsillopharyngitis




### <u>Exanthem</u> phase [[5]](/library/rXdfzo0)




* <u>Rash</u> manifests 12–48 hours after <u>fever</u> onset. [[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Fine, <u>erythematous</u>, sandpaper‑like texture

* Blanches with pressure, but nonblanching <u>petechiae</u> may also be present

* Often pruritic

* Begins on neck or trunk and spreads rapidly across the body (except for the palms and soles)

* Characteristic features include:

* Flushed cheeks with perioral <u>pallor</u>

* Strawberry tongue: bright red <u>tongue</u> color with <u>papillary</u> <u>hyperplasia</u>, which may initially be covered with a white coating

* Pastia lines

* A characteristic sign of scarlet <u>fever</u>

* Linear, <u>petechial</u> appearance

* Most pronounced in the groin, underarm, and <u>elbow</u> creases (i.e., flexural areas)

* Lasts ∼ 7 days [[1]](/library/j6d_kI0)





> [!TIP]
> Findings such as <u>coryza</u>, <u>rhinorrhea</u>, <u>cough</u>, <u>hoarseness</u>, <u>anterior</u> <u>stomatitis</u>, <u>conjunctivitis</u>, and ulcerative lesions are atypical for scarlet <u>fever</u> and warrant further investigation.

### Desquamation phase [[5]](/library/rXdfzo0)




* Desquamation;  begins 7–10 days after <u>rash</u> resolves.  [[7]](/library/bUXHbx)

* Most affected areas include the face, <u>skin</u> folds, hands, and feet.

* Lasts up to 4–6 weeks [[5]](/library/rXdfzo0)





![Desquamation in scarlet fever](media/dfm53cch3dp9ch5zu2vc2hep.jpg)

## Diagnosis

Scarlet <u>fever</u> can rarely occur after nonpharyngeal infection; for management in those cases, see “<u>Impetigo</u>” and/or “<u>Nonpurulent skin and soft tissue infections</u>.”




### <u>Confirmatory tests</u> [[1]](/library/j6d_kI0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)




Scarlet <u>fever</u> has characteristic clinical features, but the diagnosis must be confirmed with one of the following <u>laboratory studies</u>. For <u>acute pharyngitis</u> without the other clinical features of scarlet <u>fever</u>, see “<u>Diagnosis of acute pharyngitis</u>.”




* <u>Throat culture for GAS</u> (<u>gold standard</u>)

* Rapid <u>antigen</u> detection testing (<u>rapid strep test</u>)

* Positive test: Treat as scarlet <u>fever</u>.

* Negative test 

* Adults: No further testing is routinely required.

* Children > 3 years of age: Obtain a <u>throat culture for GAS</u>.

* Children ≤ 3 years of age: Consider obtaining a <u>throat culture for GAS</u>.  [[1]](/library/j6d_kI0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[8]](/library/BMYzIp)

* <u>NAAT</u> from a throat swab [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Delayed presentation with <u>nonsuppurative complications of GAS infection</u>: <u>antistreptolysin O</u> (<u>ASO</u>) and <u>anti-DNase B</u> (<u>ADB</u>) <u>titers</u>  [[8]](/library/BMYzIp)[[9]](/library/kobmXu)





> [!TIP]
> Blood tests are not routinely recommended as common findings (e.g., <u>leukocytosis</u>, raised <u>inflammatory markers</u>) are nonspecific. [[10]](/library/N6d-OI0)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Other <u>infectious rashes in childhood</u>

* <u>Drug hypersensitivity reaction</u>

* <u>Chickenpox</u> (<u>varicella</u>)

* <u>Kawasaki disease</u>

* <u>Viral tonsillitis</u> (<u>infectious mononucleosis</u>, <u>herpangina</u>)

## Treatment

Scarlet <u>fever</u> can rarely occur after nonpharyngeal infection; for management in those cases, see “<u>Impetigo</u>” and/or “<u>Nonpurulent skin and soft tissue infections</u>.”




* Initiate one of the <u>recommended antibiotic regimens for acute GAS pharyngitis</u>, e.g.: [[1]](/library/j6d_kI0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Oral <u>penicillin V</u> or <u>amoxicillin</u>

* <u>Nonsevere penicillin reaction</u>: oral <u>cephalosporins</u> (e.g., <u>cephalexin</u>)

* <u>Severe penicillin reaction</u>: oral <u>macrolides</u> (e.g., <u>azithromycin</u>) or <u>clindamycin</u>

* Recommend <u>supportive care for sore throats</u>.

* Isolation recommendations [[1]](/library/j6d_kI0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Hospitalized patients: Maintain <u>droplet precautions</u> for 24 hours after initiating <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* Advise outpatients to isolate until they:

* Are afebrile

* Have been taking <u>antibiotic therapy</u> for at least 12–24 hours





> [!TIP]
> <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> reduces symptom duration, infectiousness, and risk of developing <u>complications of scarlet fever</u>. [[1]](/library/j6d_kI0)




![Pediatric Rashes – Part 2: Treatment](media/small_5dfa15d1505dd.jpg)

Pediatric Rashes – Part 2: Treatment

## Complications

* Scarlet <u>fever</u> is considered a nonsuppurative (i.e., non-<u>pus</u>-forming) complication of <u>streptococcal</u> tonsillopharyngitis.

* Other complications of <u>GAS tonsillopharyngitis</u> may occur during or after scarlet <u>fever</u>, especially in patients who did not receive <u>antibiotic therapy</u>. E.g.:

* <u>Nonsuppurative complications of GAS infection</u> (e.g., <u>poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis</u>, <u>acute rheumatic fever</u>)

* <u>Suppurative complications of acute tonsillopharyngitis</u> (e.g., <u>retropharyngeal abscess</u>, <u>peritonsillar abscess</u>)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
